To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the membrane-active peptide maculatin 2.1 (M2.1) adopts a kinked alpha-helix when bound to the membrane and that the mechanism of lysis is likely to involve membrane curvature rather than pore formation.
M1.1 spontaneously inserts into membranes to form TM clusters, and that these aggregates are not pore-forming but rather induce membrane curvature and lysis.

1) the minimum size of a transmembraneous aggregate is just four peptides, 2) there is no central pore-like structure in these aggregates, 3) the aggregates exclude lipid headgroups, 4) the aggregates are stable in the presence of lipid headgroups, and 5) the aggregates do not induce a significant change in the lipid bilayer properties, such as the area per lipid or the bilayer thickness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a new coarse-grained model of the membrane-active AMP maculatin 2.1.
understanding the molecular basis of the mechanism of action of the antimicrobial peptide maculatin 2.1.
the mechanism of membrane-destabilizing activity of M1.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the mechanism of membrane-destabilizing activity of M1. 1.1 involves a combination of interfacial and TM peptide aggregation, with the membrane-destabilization activity arising primarily from induced membrane curvature.
the membrane lysis mechanism of M1. 1.1 is not yet clear.
the mechanism of membrane-lysing activity for M1.1 involves both peptide-induced curvature and TM peptide aggregates.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
M1.1 adopts an interfacial location on the membrane surface at low peptide/lipids ratios, but at higher ratios it inserts into the membrane to form aggregates.
M1.1 is capable of forming a stable, membrane-lytic aggregate that can induce membrane permeabilization by a mechanism that is not well understood.

the peptide/lipids systems simulated here are consistent with a mechanism in which the initial binding and membrane perturbation of M1. 1.1 by monomeric peptides is followed by the formation of TM aggregates that induce membrane curvature and lysis.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the membrane lytic mechanism of AMPs is likely to be complex and multifaceted, involving a range of peptide-lipid and lipid-lipid interactions, and that a pore-like mechanism is unlikely to explain the membrane lysis of many AMPs, including M1.1.
the mechanism by which the AMP M1.1 lyses membranes appears to be fundamentally different from that of WALP, a well-characterized model peptide.

the mechanism of M1. 1.1-mediated permeabilization involves a cooperative, multistep insertion process, in which membrane-active peptides form TM clusters that induce membrane curvature and/or disruption.
